I am seventy-five years old, and I have farmed this land in Quzhou for half a century. I never went to school, but the land and the sky have been my teachers. My household has six people; my sons and their wives work in the factory in town, so my wife and I do the daily farm work, with the grandchildren helping during school holidays. I have fourteen mu and a well that has never run dry.

This year, I will put nine mu into the wheat-maize rotation and five mu into cotton. I do not gamble on new fads. Wheat and maize are my backbone—they fill our bellies and the grain station always buys them. Cotton brings in cash, but at my age the picking is hard on my back, so five mu is enough to cover medicine and school fees without breaking me.

For the wheat on those nine mu: I sowed it last October with improved seed from the township store—varieties like Shixin or Lumai that I have trusted for years. Now that spring is here, I will irrigate four times before harvest: green-up, jointing, heading, and grain filling. I spread compound fertilizer at the base and topdress with urea at jointing—altogether about sixteen kilograms of nitrogen, six of phosphorus, and four of potassium per mu. I spray three times: once for weeds and twice for insects or rust if the weather turns damp. I rotary-tilled before sowing in autumn. If no late frost comes, I expect about seven hundred and fifty jin per mu.

For the summer maize on the same nine mu: The day after we cut the wheat in early June, I sow hybrid maize immediately—Denghai 605 or Zhengdan 958. The summer season is short, barely one hundred days, so I do not waste time deep-ploughing; I use no-tillage or a light rotary pass and plant right away. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing—about fourteen kilograms of nitrogen, five of phosphorus, and four of potassium per mu. I irrigate twice: once if June is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage. Three pesticide sprays for armyworm and weeds. With good summer rain, I can harvest one thousand jin per mu.

For the five mu of cotton: In April I plough deeply because cotton roots need loose, deep soil. I plant hybrid Guoxinmian seed, about three jin per mu. I apply fertilizer at sowing and again at budding—about twelve kilograms of nitrogen, five of phosphorus, and five of potassium per mu total. I irrigate three times: at budding, flowering, and boll opening. Cotton pests never sleep; I spray about twelve times through the season for bollworm, aphids, and mites. I expect around six hundred and fifty jin of seed cotton per mu.

Why this plan? At my age, stability is worth more than profit. I use improved and hybrid seeds because I have lived long enough to see they yield better than the old grains my father grew. I save time by not ploughing the maize field deeply. I use my well water carefully, only at the critical stages when the crop is thirsty. This is how I have survived fifty years on this plain.

decision.reasoning_summary: I have farmed these Quzhou fields for fifty years and at seventy-five I trust what I know. I keep nine mu in the reliable wheat-maize rotation for food security and sure buyers, and five mu in cotton for cash income. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize and cotton varieties because I have seen them outperform traditional seeds with my own eyes. Wheat gets rotary tillage, four irrigations, and three sprays; maize is no-tilled after wheat harvest with two irrigations and three sprays to beat the short summer window; cotton is deeply ploughed in spring and needs three irrigations and twelve pesticide applications to fight bollworm and aphids.
